title: Same latitude, different seasons
question: Why can places in the same temperate band have such different weather?
hook: Two cities can sit at the same distance from the equator, yet one has mild, damp winters while the other freezes and then bakes.
idea: Temperate climates are shaped by sea currents, winds, landmass size and altitude, not just by how far they are from the equator.

beats.prompt: A temperate town sits where air flows onshore from a cool ocean to its west. What are its seasons like?

choices.label: Hot summers and bitterly cold winters
choices.feedback: That pattern comes from large land masses, not from steady onshore ocean air.

choices.label: Mild summers, cool but not cold winters, rain all year
A dry summer and a wet winter
choices.feedback: That is the Mediterranean pattern, set by nearby deserts in summer.

choices.label: A long dry winter and a very wet summer
choices.feedback: That is a monsoon pattern, not the effect of cool ocean air.

beats.explain: Onshore flow from cool high-latitude oceans gives oceanic climates mild summers, cool winters, and humidity and rain spread through the year.

beats.prompt: Put these zones in order, moving from the equator toward a pole.
items: Subtropical part of the temperate zone (23.5° to 35°)
beats.explain: The temperate zone spans between the tropics and the polar regions; its subtropical band lies between 23.5° and 35°, and its cooler band between 35° and 66.5°.

beats.prompt: Sort each climate into its part of the temperate zone.
beats.explain: Some classifications split the temperate zone into a subtropical zone of humid subtropical and Mediterranean climates and a cool temperate zone of oceanic and continental climates.

beats.prompt: Match each climate to a region where it is found.
beats.explain: Each temperate climate type turns up in particular regions spread across several continents.
